sentences.t: More than 200 residents came to the meeting and the supervisors voted it down.

In the week before November 18, 2025 the Hazle Township board of supervisors, in Luzerne County, unanimously rejected NorthPoint Development's land application for Project Hazelnut, a data center campus beside the north zone of the Humboldt Industrial Park.

The stated ground was procedural: data centers were not specifically permitted on the property, and the application should have gone first to the zoning hearing board for a special exception, which had not happened.

Ginny Marcille-Kerslake, the eastern Pennsylvania senior organiser for Food and Water Watch, which worked with residents on the campaign, said: "There is a reason why communities are pushing back on data centers, with residents showing up and speaking out, filling township meeting rooms in opposition: they serve private interests at the expense of the community."
Before the vote, the company had been asking the county for a tax break.

NorthPoint sought Local Economic Revitalization Tax Assistance relief on county real estate taxes at 90 per cent for the first seven years, tapering to 80, 70 and 60, with payments in lieu of $2,500 an acre for land carrying buildings; township and school district breaks had already been approved.
The phased payments were set out as 211.65 acres on January 31, 2026 for $529,125, 97.54 acres on July 1, 2026 for $243,850 and 164.26 acres on January 1, 2027 for $410,650.

Tom Williams and Brian Stahl spoke for NorthPoint; the county infrastructure committee, chaired by Jimmy Sabatino with Harry Haas and Patty Krushnowski, sent the request on to a council work session on March 11.

The company's account of the buildings was that they would be air cooled, possibly using grey water from the West Hazleton treatment plant, with diesel generators for backup, and that the noise would be like a dull conversation.
It put permanent employment at about 900.
The project is recorded as cancelled, on 1,280 acres with 15 buildings, with pushback confirmed at high confidence and Food and Water Watch as the group.

Hazle Township has since adopted zoning limits running from June 8, 2026 to December 5, 2026, and four other municipalities nearby have done the same; Madison Township has a full moratorium from June 1, 2026 to June 1, 2027.

Nine other recorded data center sites sit within 39 kilometres, including an Amazon proposal at Kline Township seven kilometres off and a 350 megawatt Keel Infrastructure campus under construction at Panther Creek at 16.

unconfirmed: The Food and Water Watch account is dated November 18, 2025 and refers to the vote as having happened at the prior week's meeting without giving its date; the page had it as Friday, November 15, 2025, which was in fact a Saturday, so the date has come out. That account gives neither the building count nor the acreage, which are our record's. A further sentence attributed to Food and Water Watch, that data centers "risk strapping Pennsylvanians with high electricity bills, lower quality of life, health and environmental impacts, while developers and fossil fuel corporations stand to profit", is not in the page read here, and the organiser's own words are quoted instead. The Times Leader report on the tax break carries no year for the March 11 work session, and its phased payment dates run into 2026 and 2027, after the rejection; whether the tax request came before the rejection or whether NorthPoint pressed on afterwards is unresolved, and the sequence as written may be wrong. No resident or supervisor is named in either report. No megawatt or water figure has been published for a 1,280 acre campus. The 2822news report and the Data Center Dynamics report in our record were not fetched.

sentences.t: The quarry was going to be warehouses.

HCI DP Land Acquisition LLC, tied to the Hanover Company, proposes data centers on a 250 acre former quarry off Wagner Street in South Hanover Township, Dauphin County, part of the township's industrial park and owned by the construction materials firm Pennsy Supply.

The first plans were for two single storey buildings of 401,800 and 195,000 square feet with an electricity substation, and a second request covers an adjacent parcel not currently zoned for industry.
By June the plans had grown.

A group calling itself Protect South Hanover Township, Hummelstown and Hershey says HCI submitted a noise study on June 8, 2026 showing eight proposed buildings, and that the zoning hearing board proceedings have been postponed indefinitely at HCI's request.

The group's objections are noise it says travels up to 2.5 miles, hazardous pollutants from diesel generators, water use and contamination, heat, electricity rates, and housing prices it says drop an average of 5 to 20 per cent near a data center.
It also says the full health and environmental impacts of data centers are largely unknown.
Nobody is named on the site as running the campaign.
The project is recorded as proposed on 250 acres with no capacity, no cost and no developer field filled in, and pushback marked unknown.
A residents' group with a website, a noise study and a postponed hearing is not unknown pushback.
The address on record is Hummelstown; the township taking the decisions is South Hanover, and Hershey is next door.
The 803 megawatt Crane Clean Energy Center is 14 kilometres away and the 1,411 megawatt Brunner Island plant 20.
The Harrisburg golf course scheme is 11 kilometres off, a cancelled South Annville project 16 and a Fairview Crossroads proposal 17.

unconfirmed: The campaign site is an advocacy source and its figures for noise travel and house price falls are its own claims rather than verified findings. The Data Center Dynamics report in our record is not fetchable, so the building sizes, the quarry ownership and the second parcel are attributed to our record's source list. The Fox43 report on a court fight was not fetched, and what is before the court, and when, is unestablished. No megawatt, water or cost figure has been published, and no HCI or Hanover Company representative is quoted. Whether the eight building plan has been formally filed is unknown.

sentences.t: The board turned it down five to nothing, and the reason was a substation on the wrong side of the street.

Breaker Street Associates LLC proposed nearly 1.1 million square feet of data centers on 131 acres on the south side of Breaker Street between Hill Street and the Casey Highway in Jessup, Lackawanna County: six buildings 130 feet tall, drawing 600 megawatts.
The data centers themselves fell in mixed use zoning south of Breaker Street, but the switchyard and substation fell on residentially zoned land to the north.
The Jessup zoning hearing board voted unanimously to deny the application on December 23, 2025, and issued its written decision on January 2, 2026.
The five members were chairman Jeff Smith, Angela Muchal, Rella Scassellati, Barbara Bzdick and Andrew Tomaskevich, sitting with the board solicitor Mario J. Hanyon.
They held that the substation was not a public utility facility under Pennsylvania law because the proposed use is not, in the decision's words, "to or for the public for compensation".
This land has been fought over before.

Breaker Street was previously the site of a contested warehouse proposal, which Jessup stopped by applying stricter zoning in 2019, and which brought lawsuits from the property owner and the developer William Rinaldi.
Breaker Street Associates shares an address with Catalyst Commercial Development, whose principal Gabe Clark signed the zoning application.
The developer may appeal to county court.
The project is recorded as proposed at 600 megawatts on 131 acres, and pushback marked unknown.

Lackawanna County holds 13 data center sites on record, and ten sit within 13 kilometres of this one, including a Catalyst proposal at one kilometre, a withdrawn Blakely campus at four and the Archbald cluster at four and five.
The 1,362 megawatt Lackawanna Energy Center is a kilometre away.

unconfirmed: No resident is quoted in the report read here and it does not describe any public opposition, so the size of the local response is unknown. Whether Breaker Street Associates has appealed to the Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas is unknown. The 2019 warehouse history, the shared address with Catalyst Commercial Development and Gabe Clark's signature on the zoning application come from a syndicated Times-Tribune report that was not fetched directly and are attributed to our record's source list; the report read here does not mention Clark. No water figure, cost or end user has been published. Our record's status of proposed predates the denial.

sentences.t: It is the same company as the one down the road, under a different name.

Catalyst Commercial Development LLC filed a land development application on August 13 for a 487,000 square foot data center near Sunnyside Road and Alberigi Drive in Jessup, beside the Lackawanna Energy Center gas plant, on 48 acres by the record's count.
Catalyst's principal is Gabe Clark, who signed the zoning application for the 600 megawatt Breaker Street proposal a kilometre away, and the two firms share an address.
The site was going to be a warehouse.
The record's own source is an archived Times-Tribune report headlined that a developer has shifted from warehouse to data center by the power plant in Jessup, dated September 16, 2025.
Reporters could not get Catalyst to comment.
No megawatt figure, water figure, cost or tenant has been published for the Sunnyside Road building.
The project is recorded as proposed on 48 acres at high confidence, and pushback marked unknown.

Ten other recorded data center sites sit within 14 kilometres: Breaker Street at one, a withdrawn Blakely campus at four, Archbald at five, Project Green Mountain at five, and Project Gravity, Project North and Project Scott at six.
Jessup borough has no moratorium on record.
Mayfield adopted zoning limits on December 10, 2025, Susquehanna County on December 29, Olyphant Borough on April 14, 2026, and Clinton Township a full moratorium on April 30.
The 1,362 megawatt Lackawanna Energy Center is a kilometre away and the 72 megawatt Archbald power station two.

unconfirmed: The year of the August 13 filing is not stated in the report read here, though the context is 2025, and that report does not name Gabe Clark or give the acreage; both come from our record's source list, as does the warehouse history in the archived Times-Tribune report, which was not fetched. Whether the land development application has been decided is unknown. No resident, borough official or company representative is quoted, and Catalyst did not respond to the reporting.

sentences.t: A well driller told the meeting there is not enough water here.

Mele Brothers Realty, a Montgomery County firm, wants to build a data center campus on about 750 acres at Route 903 and Maury Road in Penn Forest Township, Carbon County, in a place better known for vacation homes and woods.
Tim Hendricks told the township last September that he was under agreement to purchase the land.

On March 2, 2026 the township supervisors, Roger Meckes, Christian Bartulovich, Brandon Bell, Patrick Holland and James Denier, unanimously approved a 45 page curative zoning amendment to regulate data centers.

It sets a minimum lot area of 30 acres, a height cap of 60 feet plus 15 for rooftop equipment, architectural and design standards, setback, buffer yard and equipment screening rules, noise and vibration standards, an emergency response plan, a power feasibility study, a water feasibility study with well testing, a limit of 50 per cent on woodland disturbance, a decommissioning plan with a cost estimate, and a public website giving 24 hours' notice before the backup generators run.
Vice chairman Christian Bartulovich said: 'We've written an ordinance that is as expansive as is legally possible to write.'
Jacob Peterzak of Mayer's Well Drilling said: "There is not enough groundwater in this area to provide for a data center."
Linda Christman, president of Save Carbon County, said: "If they are thinking of putting a data center in Penn Forest, they should price in the cost of aggravation."
The resident Ashleigh Davis went at the groundwater rule: "How are we going to determine where the aquifer spanned to?"
The developer's attorney is Matthew McHugh.

Earlier meetings had turned on where the cooling water would come from and what it would do to residents' wells, alongside noise, electrical infrastructure and what an industrial site would mean for a place whose identity is tourism.
The site is about four miles from the Lehigh Gorge Scenic Railway.

The project is recorded as proposed on 750 acres with no capacity and no developer field filled in, pushback marked confirmed, with a Facebook group called Penn Forest Residents Against Data Center attached.
The nearest generation is the 80 megawatt Panther Creek plant 17 kilometres off, where Keel Infrastructure is building a 350 megawatt campus.

unconfirmed: The developer's name in our record is blank; Mele Brothers Realty is named in the report read here as the Montgomery County company that owns the land along Route 903 and Maury Road, and the description of it as being of Glenside comes from search summaries of WFMZ and Times News reports that were not fetched. Tim Hendricks's relationship to Mele Brothers is not established. A line attributed to Ashleigh Davis, that the ordinance "is what is going to protect us in the future", is not in that report and has come out. No megawatt, water or cost figure has been published. Whether Mele Brothers has filed an application under the new ordinance, and whether it has challenged the ordinance, are unknown. The 750 acre figure is the tract said to be under agreement, not a plan area.

sentences.t: One county commissioner told the room he put the chances of it being built at less than one in five.

Keel Infrastructure, the company that was Bitfarms until it rebranded on April 1 and moved its domicile from Canada to the United States, says the Scrubgrass site near Kennerdell in Venango County could become its largest long term AI data center campus.
The site is the old Scrubgrass Generating Plant, a waste coal burner on about 650 acres in Scrubgrass Township, bought from Stronghold Digital Mining in March 2025.
It has direct access to 85 megawatts, with talk of scaling to 1.3 gigawatts through grid imports.
About 40 residents from southern Venango County came to Room 100 of the county courthouse annex on the afternoon of Tuesday, June 16, 2026.
Scott Gearhart, who lives in Scrubgrass Township, asked: "Who knew about it? Why here? What is the impact going to be on area residents and the environment? How far along are the plans?"
Sandra McStraw made the jobs point: "The data center would only generate a few jobs for technicians."
Mallory Piercy, a lawyer from Rockland, told the commissioners: "We are concerned not hearing from you that you are against it, as we are."
Commissioner Ken Bryan answered: "Where the county is at now is we have the same concerns as everyone in this room. We are not for or against the data center."

Commissioner Tim Heffernan went further: "This is probably going to be unpopular and not what you want to hear, but there is an incredible amount of speculation on data centers right now," and put the odds of it being built at less than 20 per cent.
Jim Miller chairs the county regional planning commission and Jenna Dillion is its deputy director.

Residents raised electricity use that would exceed everything the county's homes use now, water consumption, pollution and the effect on their wells, noise, and what it would mean for Emlenton, Rockland and Victory townships around it.
The record used to list the site as operating at 63 megawatts; it now says proposed, and still marks pushback as unknown, at high confidence.
A packed county meeting is not unknown pushback, and the 63 megawatts does not match either the 85 the company advertises or the gigawatt it talks about.
The 83 megawatt Scrubgrass coal refuse plant is on the site and the 268 megawatt Handsome Lake gas plant is two kilometres away.
The only other site recorded within 40 kilometres is Iron Mountain's Boyers facility, 21 kilometres off.

unconfirmed: The acreage, the 85 megawatt access, the 1.3 gigawatt ambition, the Stronghold purchase and the April 1 rebrand come from search summaries of company filings, trade coverage and the exploreClarion and northwiseproject write-ups, which were not fetched, and are attributed to our record's source list. The year of the April 1 rebrand is given in those summaries as 2026 but is unconfirmed. A question attributed to Sandra McStraw, "what economic incentive would out weigh our concerns as citizens?", is not in the report read here, and the line quoted above is hers instead. No Keel representative is quoted. No water figure, cost or timetable has been published, and no application to any municipality has been reported. Coal refuse is classified as a Tier II alternative energy source under Pennsylvania law, which is background rather than a finding about this project.

sentences.t: The plans arrived on a Friday afternoon, two days before the supervisors were to vote on shutting the door.

PA Data Center Partners filed at 3.34pm on Friday, July 10, 2026 for a data center off Loop Road in Granville Township, Mifflin County, on farmland between the road and the Mifflin County Industrial Park that acts as a buffer between the park and houses along the Juniata River.
Renderings show six buildings against the industrial park, with planting on the neighbourhood side.

The supervisors had called a special meeting for Sunday, July 14 to start a curative amendment, the process that lets a municipality declare its own zoning ordinance invalid where it fails to provide for a lawful use, and which holds off competing landowner amendments while a new ordinance is written.
The record shows Granville Township zoning limits running from July 12, 2026 to January 8, 2027, with the note that they were enacted two days after the application was submitted.
About 100 people came to the emergency meeting.
Several speakers asked Granville to become the first Pennsylvania municipality to take a stand against large scale data center development.

Tony Dastra, the Green Party candidate for governor, told them: "It takes just one voice, one person, one municipality to stand up for the people. This municipality could be that one, to not only protect its own community but protect communities like mine. We all across the state need some municipality to step up."
The resident Nate Fisher made the narrower point: "What was presented Friday is only plans for a proposed data center that have to go through other steps to be approved. There may be hope yet."
The township solicitor Fred Lighty advised against the curative amendment.
The developer's appeal goes to the Granville Township zoning hearing board at 7pm on October 1 at the township building.
Two of the parcels named in the reporting are owned by Kevin and Lisa Oberholtzer, near the Walmart off Middle Road, and by Mark Ellinger and Nancy Collins at 841 Loop Road, Lewistown.
The project is recorded as proposed with no acreage, no capacity, no cost and no developer field filled in, and pushback marked unknown.
This is the only data center site recorded in Mifflin County; the nearest other is a Centre WISP building 34 kilometres away, and the nearest generation is a 100 megawatt solar farm at 48 kilometres.

unconfirmed: The report read here gives no acreage, building count, megawatt, water or cost figure, and the six building rendering and the buffer description come from search summaries of the ABC27 and Data Center Dynamics reports that were not fetched, attributed to our record's source list; it does not name the developer either. The 180 days the curative amendment would allow is our record's figure and is not in it. The October 1 zoning hearing board date comes from our record's source list. Whether the supervisors pursued the curative amendment against their solicitor Fred Lighty's advice, and what the July 12 zoning limits in our record actually say, are unresolved. A developer trading as Pennsylvania Data Center Partners is separately reported as building a three campus, 1.3 gigawatt scheme called PAX-1 at Middlesex Township in Cumberland County; whether it is the same company is unestablished. No company representative is quoted.

sentences.t: There is a gas plant and an industrial park; whether there is a data center is another matter.

Imperial Land Corporation is developing the Fort Cherry Development District in Robinson Township, northern Washington County, off the Southern Beltway near Pittsburgh International Airport and the Shell cracker plant.

Phase one has been built and holds three pad ready sites; at completion the company anticipates six million square feet of industrial and flex space, with sites up to 100 acres and buildings from 20,000 to over a million square feet.
The power came first.

Liberty Energy, Range Resources and Imperial Land signed a strategic agreement to build a natural gas generation facility at Fort Cherry aimed at the data center sector and other heavy electricity users, which the partners say will make the district a prime location for future industrial demand.

Imperial Land says the development is projected to generate over $750 million in private investment, and that it has put in more than $5 million of its own for planning, engineering and infrastructure, extended sewer lines and donated land for a treatment plant.

The entry stands as under construction at 1,000 megawatts on 875 acres costing $750 million, with Liberty Energy and Imperial Land Corporation as developers, pushback confirmed as organised advocacy, and the Center for Coalfield Justice as the group.
The $750 million in the cost field is the company's projection of total private investment across a six million square foot industrial district, not the cost of a data center.
Nothing in the company's account names a data center operator, a building, a tenant or a start date.
The record's address is McDonald; the township is Robinson.

Washington County holds four data center sites on record and ten sit within 32 kilometres of this one, including a Prime Data Centers gas powered campus at 16, a 700 megawatt CNX land advertisement at Zediker Station at 22 and Aligned's 2,000 megawatt Project Phoenix at 32.

Eight municipalities within reach have acted, all but one with zoning limits rather than pauses: Bell Acres Borough back on March 13, 2023, Union Township on June 10, 2025, South Strabane on February 4, 2026, Shippingport on March 4, Adams Township on July 13, Lancaster Township on July 21, Smith Township with no date, and a full moratorium at Upper Burrell from May 15 to November 11, 2026 with the TECfusions site grandfathered in.

For all the talk of power here, the existing generation is not close: the 262 megawatt Brunot Island plant is 21 kilometres off and the 1,808 megawatt Beaver Valley nuclear station 32, which is the argument for building gas on site.

unconfirmed: The developer's own page is the only source read, so the description of the district is the company's account of itself. The Liberty Energy and Range Resources agreement comes from a Data Center Dynamics report that is not fetchable and is attributed to our record's source list; the size of the gas plant is not established. Nothing describing organised opposition to this specific project was found, although our record marks it as organised advocacy with the Center for Coalfield Justice, and that group's involvement is unconfirmed. The 875 acres and the 1,000 megawatts in our record could not be traced to any source read. Whether any data center has been proposed, permitted or begun at Fort Cherry is unknown.

sentences.t: It is a small building from about 1980, refurbished in 2008, and it changed hands for $7.12 million.

Ardent Data Centers, part of Northern Data Group, bought the 41,000 square foot data center at 615 McMichael Road in McKees Rocks, in Allegheny County, on 7.5 acres, and set out to take it from 5 megawatts to 20 by the second half of 2025.
Northern Data split itself into three brands in the summer of 2023: Taiga Cloud for GPU rental, Ardent for data centers and Peak Mining for cryptocurrency.
Taiga runs more than 20,000 GPUs by the company's own account, and Peak Mining has been developing a 30 megawatt site at Grand Forks, North Dakota and two 300 megawatt sites at Corpus Christi, Texas.
By January 2026 Northern Data had agreed to be bought by Rumble for $767 million.
The building is recorded as operating at 20 megawatts costing $7.12 million, at high confidence, and pushback marked unknown.
The $7.12 million is the purchase price, not a construction cost.
This is an ordinary colocation building in a county filling up with much larger schemes.

Allegheny County holds eight sites on record, and ten sit within 29 kilometres, including DataBank at four, two small Expedient buildings at nine and 12, the Fort Cherry district at 13, a 496 megawatt Five 9s land advertisement at Aliquippa at 23 and a 700 megawatt CNX advertisement at 29.
Ten municipalities within reach have adopted zoning limits or a moratorium, from Bell Acres Borough in March 2023 to Lancaster Township in July 2026.
The 262 megawatt Brunot Island plant is nine kilometres away and the 1,808 megawatt Beaver Valley nuclear station 32.

unconfirmed: The Data Center Dynamics report in our record is not fetchable and the press release and directory pages were not fetched, so no source url is listed and each sentence is attributed to our record's source list. Whether the building actually reached 20 megawatts is unconfirmed; our record carries 20 while the reporting describes it as a plan for the second half of 2025. Whether the Rumble acquisition has closed, and what it means for this site, is unknown. No resident, official or company representative is quoted, and no water figure has been published.

sentences.t: This was a bitcoin mine, and the company has changed its name to match where it is going.

Mawson Infrastructure Group runs a data center and bitcoin mining site at 950 10th Street in Midland, Beaver County, and rebranded as Big Digital Energy in April 2026 as it moved from pure cryptocurrency mining towards AI and high performance computing.
In April 2024 it announced an expansion of the Midland facilities to 120 megawatts and 38,810 miners, taking the company's total to about 129 megawatts and 41,530 miners.
The site is now described as 120 megawatts.
The entry is recorded as operating and expanding at 144 megawatts, at high confidence, and marks pushback as unknown.
The 144 does not match the 120 in the reporting, and which is current is unresolved.
Beaver County is becoming one of the denser corners of this map.

Aligned Data Centers' 2,000 megawatt Project Phoenix is three kilometres away, a 496 megawatt Five 9s land advertisement at Aliquippa 18, a proposed data center at the Sammis power plant site 19, and a Prime Data Centers gas powered campus 23.
The 1,808 megawatt Beaver Valley nuclear station is two kilometres from the building, the Shell cracker plant's 257 megawatts 11 and the 1,210 megawatt South Field plant across the state line 19.
Shippingport, where the nuclear station sits, adopted zoning limits on March 4, 2026, and seven other municipalities within reach have done the same.
The record's six sources include a company news page, a press release wire and a global energy monitor wiki entry.
Three are the company describing itself, which is worth knowing when reading the megawatt figures.

unconfirmed: The Post-Gazette and CBS Pittsburgh reports in our record were not fetched, the Data Center Dynamics report is not fetchable, and the company pages were not opened, so no source url is listed and each sentence is attributed to our record's source list. No resident, borough official or company representative is quoted, and no account of any local response in Midland was found. No water figure, cost or employment figure has been published. Whether any AI or high performance computing load has actually been installed at Midland, as opposed to announced, is unknown. Our record's status of operating and expanding is not tied to a dated source that could be read.
